chapters.1: Zechariah calls the returned exiles to turn back to God rather than repeat their ancestors' mistakes. He then describes a night vision of horsemen patrolling the earth and reporting it is at rest, followed by a vision of four horns that scattered Judah and four craftsmen coming to break their power.
chapters.2: Zechariah sees a man measuring Jerusalem for rebuilding, and an angel announces the city will grow so large it cannot be walled, with God himself as a protective wall of fire around it. God promises to punish the nations that scattered his people and to dwell among them again, drawing other nations to join them.
chapters.3: In a vision, the high priest Joshua stands before God in filthy clothes with Satan accusing him, but God rebukes Satan and has Joshua's clothes changed to clean garments, symbolizing forgiveness. God promises to bring his servant called "the Branch" and to remove the guilt of the land in a single day.
chapters.4: Zechariah sees a golden lampstand flanked by two olive trees, which is explained as a message to the leader Zerubbabel that the temple will be rebuilt not by human strength but by God's Spirit. The vision assures that despite small, discouraging beginnings, the work will be completed.
chapters.5: Zechariah sees a flying scroll symbolizing a curse that will fall on thieves and those who swear falsely, cleansing the land of such sin. He then sees a woman representing wickedness sealed inside a basket and carried away to Babylon, showing evil being removed from the land.
chapters.6: Four chariots with different colored horses go out to patrol the earth on God's behalf. Zechariah is then told to crown the high priest Joshua as a sign pointing to "the Branch," a coming figure who will build the temple and rule as both king and priest.
chapters.7: People ask whether they should continue a fast kept during the exile, and God responds that their fasting had become self-serving rather than genuine devotion to him. He reminds them that true faithfulness means doing justice and showing mercy, which their ancestors refused to do, leading to their exile.
chapters.8: God promises to return to Jerusalem and restore it as a place of peace, prosperity, and old age again filled with children playing safely in the streets. He calls the people to truthfulness and justice, and predicts that many nations will one day come to seek the Lord in Jerusalem.
chapters.9: This chapter announces judgment on neighboring cities like Tyre and the Philistine towns, then shifts to the famous prophecy of a king coming to Jerusalem humbly, riding on a donkey, bringing peace rather than conquest. It closes with promises of restoration and protection for God's people.
chapters.10: God promises to strengthen and restore his scattered people, likened to a flock without a shepherd that has been let down by corrupt leaders. He pledges to regather them from exile among the nations and bring down the pride of the powers that oppressed them.
chapters.11: In a strange symbolic act, Zechariah plays the role of a shepherd who is paid a contemptuous thirty pieces of silver and then breaks his staffs, representing God's rejection of unfaithful leaders and the breaking of unity between the people. The chapter ends with a warning about a coming "worthless shepherd" who will exploit the flock instead of caring for it.
chapters.12: God promises to defend Jerusalem against nations that besiege it, giving its defenders unusual strength. The chapter also contains a striking prophecy that the people will one day look on one they have "pierced" and mourn deeply, as for a lost firstborn child.
chapters.13: God promises a cleansing fountain to deal with sin and to remove idolatry and false prophecy from the land. The chapter includes a mysterious prophecy of a shepherd being struck and the flock scattered, with a faithful remnant refined like metal through fire.
chapters.14: The book ends with a vision of a final great battle at Jerusalem in which the Lord himself intervenes to fight for the city, followed by dramatic geological and cosmic changes. The result is the Lord reigning as king over the whole earth, with all nations eventually coming to Jerusalem to worship him and everything in the city made holy.
